item.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Introduces Workload Recovery and Infrastructure Checks

Today, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod introduces workload recovery and infrastructure checks. These features catch failures sooner and raise the goodput of training workloads.

🧩 The Challenge

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin.

Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then, the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training.

Types of Failures

  • Numerical faults: A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run.
  • Hung jobs: An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
  • Cluster-level failures: Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.

🛡️ New Infrastructure Checks

The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware.

Monitoring Agents and Checks

Feature Description
Health Monitoring Agent (HMA) Watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors.
MultiNodeTrainingValidation A new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent Watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
Hung Job Detection Finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.

⚙️ Existing Resiliency Features

The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time.

  • InstanceStress: Runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices.
  • InstanceConnectivity: Runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium.

🚀 Availability

These checks run when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirm that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress.

#SageMakerHyperPod #MachineLearning #GPUComputing #Kubernetes #AWSInfrastructure

Source: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Introduces Daviator and Mixed Precision for DFT GPU Acceleration
item.description:
NVIDIA Introduces Daviator and Mixed Precision for DFT GPU Acceleration

NVIDIA has introduced two new capabilities to address performance bottlenecks in generating ground-truth data for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs): a library called Daviator for batched GPU kernels and a new mixed-precision execution layer. These updates target the high volume of density functional theory (DFT) calculations required to train next-generation models, offering up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution.

🔍 The Problem with Current GPU DFT

Training MLIPs requires tens to hundreds of millions of DFT calculations. Plane-wave DFT, primarily implemented via VASP, is the standard for this task. While VASP’s OpenACC implementation speeds up large-system calculations, it struggles with the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation.

In periodic systems with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of k-points are required. Currently, VASP processes these k-points sequentially on the GPU. For small systems, this results in significant kernel launch overhead that dominates compute time. A single-atom iron system with 752 k-points, for instance, ran 8x slower on GPU hardware than on CPU. Additionally, modern NVIDIA GPUs are increasingly optimized for lower-precision data types (FP32), while traditional DFT runs in FP64, creating a gap in available throughput.

🧩 How Daviator and Mixed Precision Work

Daviator is a library of GPU kernels that replaces sequential per-k-point processing with batched operations. Its core is a batched Davidson eigensolver that swaps sequential loops for batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This approach reduces GPU kernel launches, allowing Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) occupancy to reach near saturation. Data remains resident in GPU memory, while VASP retains ownership of the self-consistent field (SCF) loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O.

The mixed-precision execution layer enables further performance gains by leveraging GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio. This is particularly effective on inference-class and workstation GPUs, such as the RTX PRO 6000, which features a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio.

⚙️ Key Details and Benchmarks

  • Integration: Daviator is accessible through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR file. Existing VASP inputs work without modification.
  • Performance: On a projected reference dataset workload, the combination of these features shows up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution.
  • Speed-ups: Daviator overcomes OpenACC limitations, achieving over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline for a single iron atom.
  • Configuration: Users must set specific environment variables to ensure efficient kernel caching:
    • export CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/cudacache
    • export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0

🚀 Availability and Limitations

Daviator is currently available for single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage for systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl), and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) are expected in a later stage. Some GPU kernels may trigger compilation on first use depending on the batch size.

💡 Why It Matters

As AI workloads drive GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the stagnation of FP64-only code performance threatens the scalability of DFT data generation. By addressing small-system GPU inefficiency and leveraging mixed precision, these capabilities allow researchers to generate the massive datasets required for MLIP training more efficiently and at a lower cost.

#DFT #VASP #GPUComputing #HPC #MLIP #NVIDIA

Source: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam Accelerates Black Hole Interferometry Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam Accelerates Black Hole Interferometry Processing

NVIDIA has introduced cuPhoton.xBeam, a GPU-based FX correlator within the cuPhoton toolkit designed to accelerate the processing of radio astronomical data used to image black holes. Developed in collaboration with the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and the MIT Haystack Observatory, this technology addresses the significant computational demands of very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI).

🔍 Overview

Imaging distant, small-scale black holes like M87* requires capturing radio emissions from gas outside the event horizon using globally distributed telescope stations. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) links these stations to record high-speed voltage streams, producing petabytes of data that must be synchronized and correlated to reconstruct images.

🧩 How it works

Interferometry involves correlating signals from pairs of telescopes to produce complex visibilities, which sample Fourier components of the sky’s brightness. The cuPhoton.xBeam component organizes these radio signals for parallel processing on GPUs:

Feature Function
Data Indexing Indexes VDIF frames by timestamp, thread, and physical location via .vdix sidecars
Correlation Correlates signals between telescope pairs to produce complex visibilities
Data Tracking Explicitly tracks missing or invalid data without rewriting recordings

⚙️ Key details

Performance testing demonstrated significant improvements in data processing speed:

  • Execution: Processed a 10 TB dataset in 70 seconds on an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs.
  • Efficiency: Achieved a 460x speedup compared to an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds.
  • Infrastructure: Utilizes GPUDirect Storage (GDS) in compatibility mode for high-speed data ingestion.

💡 Why it matters

Future initiatives, such as the next-generation EHT (ngEHT) and the proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX), aim to improve image quality and measure the photon ring near a black hole’s shadow. The current cuPhoton.xBeam tool provides a scalable pipeline to handle the massive data rates generated by these observation arrays, enabling researchers to construct 3D gas models from visibility data.

#Astronomy #GPUComputing #Interferometry #NVIDIA #DataProcessing

Source: Run GPU-Powered Black Hole Interferometry with NVIDIA cuPhoton | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Enables Full‑Cycle AI Coding on a Single Machine
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark Enables Full‑Cycle AI Coding on a Single Machine

AI agents are changing how software gets built. Developers have moved from writing every line of code by hand to directing agents that write most of the code. Traditionally this workflow is split across a laptop, a cloud model API, and a cloud VM. NVIDIA RTX Spark consolidates the entire pipeline onto one device.

🔍 Overview

  • RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops are built specifically for AI development.
  • Powered by the NVIDIA GB10 system‑on‑a‑chip and a Blackwell GPU, the platform delivers up to 128 GB of unified memory and 1 PFLOP of FP4 AI compute.
  • The device can run coding models locally (e.g., Qwen 3.8 Flash Next) and supports the entire code‑write‑test‑deploy loop on a single PC.

🛠️ How It Works

  • Unified hardware: Grace CPU + Blackwell GPU provide the inference, fine‑tuning, and compilation horsepower required by modern AI developers.
  • Local workflow options:
    • Windows with the new Windows Developer Config (pre‑installed frameworks, muted notifications, enhanced terminal, optional side task bar).
    • Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) for identical environments and dependencies used in cloud deployments.
  • GPU‑centric workload: Development has shifted from being CPU‑bound to GPU‑bound; inference for coding agents, model fine‑tuning, and compilation now run primarily on the GPU.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Performance vs. Intel Panther Lake 12Xe:
    Metric RTX Spark vs. Intel Relative Gain
    Coding agents 4.6× faster 4.6×
    Fine‑tuning 2.7× faster 2.7×
    Code compilation 1.8× faster 1.8×
  • Local model support:
    • Qwen 3.8 Flash Next runs locally, cutting cloud token consumption.
    • MAI 1.1 Coding Flash model runs on RTX Spark.
    • Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B‑A9B 24GB (74 B parameters, 9 B active MoE) runs locally using 2‑bit quantization.
  • Ecosystem integration:
    • First native PyTorch‑CUDA build and Python 3.15 release.
    • Over 2,000 ready‑to‑use Conda packages; >97 % of the top 15 000 Python packages have Arm‑compatible versions.
    • Access to CUDA‑X libraries (FlashInfer, NeMo) and NVIDIA Skills repository for GPU‑accelerated development without deep CUDA expertise.
  • Agent compatibility:
    • GitHub Copilot, Pi, Hermes, OpenClaw optimized for RTX Spark.
    • Copilot now uses Windows ML with llama.cpp backend for seamless local AI.
    • HydraFusion prompt router upgraded for local models.
    • JetBrains adds native support for Junie Local on RTX Spark.
    • Coding agents read, edit, and test code while keeping model and source files on‑device.

🚀 Availability

  • RTX Spark is offered as both laptop and compact desktop form factors.
  • The platform works with the 150 million‑device RTX PC base and virtually all cloud providers that run on NVIDIA GPUs, allowing developers to test and deploy consistently across local and cloud environments.
  • NVIDIA partnered with Microsoft to advance the Windows on Arm developer landscape, ensuring the newest Windows Developer Config is available on RTX Spark.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Consolidates a previously distributed workflow into a single machine, eliminating the need to switch between local hardware, cloud APIs, and remote VMs.
  • Enables developers to run powerful coding agents locally, reducing reliance on external API tokens and latency.
  • Provides a GPU‑first compute stack that outperforms comparable Intel CPUs across the key tasks of coding‑agent inference, model fine‑tuning, and compilation.
  • Leverages NVIDIA’s extensive AI ecosystem so new tools and frameworks work on RTX Spark from day one, while support for other hardware arrives later.

#AIagents #NVIDIA #GPUcomputing #LocalAI

Source: Code, Test, and Deploy on One Machine with NVIDIA RTX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing

NVIDIA released cuPhoton 0.1.3, an open‑source CUDA‑X toolkit that moves the entire image‑processing path for astronomy, laser, and X‑ray data onto the GPU, collapsing wait times from seconds to minutes and enabling interactive analysis.

🔍 Overview

  • Modern observatories and high‑throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU‑bound pipelines can process it.
  • The bottleneck spans the whole path: sensor readout, point‑spread‑function (PSF) matching, subtraction, fitting, classification, and alert generation.
  • A GPU‑native path that stays on the GPU from sensor to decision is missing – cuPhoton provides exactly that.

🧩 How it Works

  • cuPhoton implements each stage of the pipeline as GPU‑accelerated building blocks, keeping data resident on the GPU.
  • Typical workflow steps include:
    1. xDataReader – Loads raw sensor data directly into GPU memory.
    2. xRep – Handles PSF‑matching and image subtraction.
    3. xPois – Performs statistical processing of photon events.
    4. xFit – Fits dual‑PSF models to dipoles produced by moving objects.
    5. xScan – Classifies detections as transients or artifacts.
    6. xRay – Specialized for time‑domain X‑ray detector analysis.
Component Role
xDataReader GPU‑resident image loading
xRep PSF‑match and subtraction
xPois Photon‑event processing
xFit Dual‑PSF fitting
xScan Classification of detections
xRay X‑ray time‑domain analysis

⚙️ Key Details

  • Performance: On workloads of hundreds of terabytes, cuPhoton achieved up to 14,900× speedup for image loading and up to 14,550× for signal processing, turning months of CPU time into minutes.
  • End‑to‑end impact: Data analytics that previously required nine months completed in four hours on GPU‑accelerated Python.
  • Latency: For kilobyte‑scale datasets, the entire pipeline runs in milliseconds or microseconds.
  • Scaling: Works on multi‑GPU, multi‑node systems such as NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and NVIDIA Vera Rubin.
  • Supported environments: cuPhoton 0.1.3 runs on Linux with Python 3.12–3.14 and CUDA 13. Building from source needs a C++17 compiler, CUDA and cuFile headers, and a re‑entrant CFITSIO installation.

🚀 Availability 

1

git clone --branch v0.1.3 --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton.git

The toolkit is open‑source and part of the NVIDIA CUDA‑X ecosystem.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Instruments like the NSF‑DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory capture a 3.2‑gigapixel exposure every 39 seconds, producing up to 20 TB of images and 10 million candidate objects per night.
  • The Prompt Processing pipeline must classify ~10,000 detections within 60–120 seconds; cuPhoton’s GPU‑resident path makes such rapid turnaround feasible.
  • By eliminating the CPU‑bound bottleneck, researchers can iterate interactively, extract insights faster, and keep pace with ever‑growing data volumes.

#GPUComputing #Astronomy #NVIDIA

Source: Faster Scientific Image Analysis with NVIDIA cuPhoton | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA launches cuOpt mPDLP, a multi‑GPU solver that speeds large LPs up to 10×
item.description:
NVIDIA launches cuOpt mPDLP, a multi‑GPU solver that speeds large LPs up to 10×

Supply‑chain networks and modern energy grids are becoming more complex, stretching existing planning tools. To keep pace, teams must evaluate larger models and cope with higher uncertainty within practical planning windows, but today’s biggest problems often take hours to converge or exceed the memory of a single GPU, creating a bottleneck for business‑critical workflows.

🔍 Overview

  • Supply‑chain problems are expanding across more SKUs, lanes, and constraints than ever before.
  • Energy grids are balancing more distributed sources in real time.
  • GPU‑accelerated decision optimization already delivers >10× speedup over CPU solvers for large‑scale linear programming (LP) problems.
  • The new cuOpt Multi‑GPU Primal‑Dual hybrid gradient for Linear Programming (mPDLP) solver pushes the limits further by solving the benchmark zib03 on multiple GPUs with a solve rate nearly 10× faster than a year before.
  • Partner applications include Kinaxis (globally constrained supply and production planning) and PSR (large‑scale energy‑system capacity‑expansion models).

🧩 How it works

  • Primal‑Dual hybrid gradient (PDLP): a first‑order, gradient‑descent‑like method that is highly parallelizable and GPU‑friendly.
  • Hot loop: Sparse Matrix‑Vector Multiplication (SpMV) followed by several map operations. All map operations are trivial to distribute across GPUs.
  • Distributed challenge: SpMV is memory‑bound; increasing bandwidth directly speeds the operation.
  • Bandwidth solutions: either wait for the next GPU generation or add more GPUs, multiplying total bandwidth.
  • Multi‑GPU distribution:
    1. Reorder the matrix to improve load balancing.
    2. Partition the matrix into sub‑blocks along rows and columns.
    3. Perform an SpMV on each sub‑block, then sum partial results to reconstruct the full output.
  • This approach builds on earlier D‑PDLP work and demonstrates the potential of multi‑GPU acceleration.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Performance: >10× speedup over CPU solvers on a single GPU; mPDLP is ~10× faster than the prior single‑GPU cuOpt version.
  • Scale: Handles the zib03 benchmark (over 104 million non‑zeros) that many solvers cannot fit in a single GPU’s memory.
  • Hardware stack:
    • NVLink – fast point‑to‑point GPU‑GPU data exchange.
    • NVSwitch – orchestrates communication among many GPUs.
  • Software stack:
    • NCCL – C/C++ library for GPU‑direct point‑to‑point and collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather, Broadcast) that leverage NVLink/NVSwitch.
  • Result: With NVLink, NVSwitch, and NCCL, multiple GPUs behave as one high‑bandwidth shared machine, keeping data on the GPU and allowing the algorithm to scale without CPU involvement.
Component Role
NVLink Fast, optimized GPU‑to‑GPU data exchange
NVSwitch Efficiently orchestrates communication among several GPUs
NCCL Provides GPU‑direct point‑to‑point and collective operations

🚀 Availability

The mPDLP solver is now part of the NVIDIA cuOpt portfolio and can be deployed on systems equipped with NVLink/NVSwitch‑enabled GPUs.

Figures illustrating solve‑time improvements and benchmark performance are available in the image list.

#LinearProgramming #GPUComputing #SupplyChain #EnergySystems

Source: Scaling Decision Optimization to 100 Million Variables and Beyond with mPDLP in NVIDIA cuOpt | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: 🔥 Unlocking the Invisible: How LLMs Process Concurrent Requests Behind the Scenes
item.description:
🔥 Unlocking the Invisible: How LLMs Process Concurrent Requests Behind the Scenes

𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮: This deep dive explores the critical distinction between prefill and decode phases in LLM token generation—revealing how different batching strategies dramatically impact performance metrics. Learn why chunked prefill can boost throughput by 50% and how to balance the inherent tradeoffs between responsiveness and efficiency in production LLM systems.

🧠 The Hidden Duality of LLM Processing

Ever wonder why your LLM chat sometimes pauses mid-sentence when another user joins? Or why the first response takes so much longer than subsequent tokens? The answer lies in understanding a fundamental duality in how Large Language Models process text.

At TNG, we manage a substantial LLM infrastructure—24 H100 GPUs supporting 50 applications, handling 5,000+ inferences hourly and generating over ten million tokens daily. This scale has taught us that performance optimization requires understanding what happens 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 the scenes when multiple users interact with these models simultaneously.

When an LLM generates text, it operates in two distinct phases:

  • 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲: Processing the entire prompt to generate the first output token
  • 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲: Generating each subsequent token one by one

📸 See illustration comparing prefill (parallel processing) versus decode (sequential processing) phases

This distinction is far more consequential than most developers realize. It shapes everything from user experience to resource utilization to overall system throughput.

⏱️ Metrics That Matter: Unpacking Latency and Throughput

The prefill/decode split directly impacts two critical performance metrics:

  1. 𝙏𝙞𝙢𝙚 𝙩𝙤 𝙛𝙞𝙧𝙨𝙩 𝙩𝙤𝙠𝙚𝙣 (prefill latency) - The initial response time
  2. 𝙏𝙞𝙢𝙚 𝙥𝙚𝙧 𝙤𝙪𝙩𝙥𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙤𝙠𝙚𝙣 (decode latency) - The cadence of subsequent tokens

For interactive applications, users get frustrated if the first token takes more than 3 seconds to appear (they might think the system is broken) or if tokens generate slower than 3-10 tokens per second (slower than comfortable reading speed).

But there’s always a tradeoff. Some non-interactive applications might prioritize total token throughput over per-request latency—like when batch-processing translations or generating summaries for an entire code repository.

🔍 Resource Utilization Reality: Prefill is compute-intensive (utilizing parallel processing across all input tokens), while decode is memory-bandwidth-limited (processing just one token at a time).

📸 See graph showing how throughput increases with concurrency until GPU compute power saturates

This fundamental difference creates fascinating dynamics when multiple requests compete for resources.

🚀 Batching Strategies: Static vs. Continuous

When multiple users hit an LLM service simultaneously, the inference engine must decide how to process these concurrent requests. Two primary approaches exist:

1. Static Batching: Simple But Inefficient

Static batching processes requests in rigid groups—waiting for the entire batch to complete before starting the next one.

📸 See illustration showing how static batching processes batches in sequence

This approach optimizes “time per output token” since decode phases run uninterrupted, but it creates terrible user experiences for anyone waiting for the next batch. Even worse, it wastes GPU resources since prefill (compute-intensive) and decode (memory-bound) operations can’t run concurrently to maximize hardware utilization.

2. Continuous Batching: More Complex But Smarter

Most modern inference engines like vLLM implement continuous batching, where:

  • Completed requests immediately free up batch slots
  • New requests enter as soon as space becomes available
  • Prefill and decode operations can run simultaneously

But this creates a new challenge: 𝘩𝘰𝘸 should prefill and decode operations share resources when running concurrently?

🧩 The Breakthrough: Chunked Prefill

The default “prefill-first” strategy prioritizes new requests, minimizing time to first token. However, this creates an unfortunate side effect: whenever a new request arrives, ongoing decode operations get interrupted—users experience this as sudden pauses in their text generation.

📸 See illustration showing how prefill operations interrupt decode operations

The elegant solution? 𝗖𝗵𝘂𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹 🔥

Rather than processing an entire prompt in one massive operation, we break it into smaller chunks. This creates multiple benefits:

  • Concurrent decode operations can progress between prefill chunks
  • Users experience slowdowns rather than complete pauses
  • 𝗧𝗼𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝘆 𝟱𝟬% by better balancing compute and memory resources

📸 See illustration showing how chunked prefill allows more decode operations to proceed

Chunk size becomes a tunable parameter to balance competing priorities:

  • 𝘚𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘳 chunks → Better decode performance (smoother token generation)
  • 𝘓𝘢𝘳𝘨𝘦𝘳 chunks → Faster time to first token

Default chunk sizes typically range from 512 to 8192 tokens, but the optimal value depends on your specific workload patterns.

🌟 Key Insights for LLM Engineers

This exploration of prefill and decode phases reveals several practical insights:

  1. Measure the right metrics - Track both time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token to get a complete performance picture

  2. Consider your application type - Interactive applications need to optimize for latency; batch applications should focus on throughput

  3. Enable chunked prefill - This single optimization can boost throughput by 50% while improving user experience

  4. Tune chunk size thoughtfully - Balance responsiveness against smoothness based on your users’ needs

The journey to optimized LLM performance doesn’t end here. In environments with unpredictable load patterns, finding the perfect chunk size remains challenging—which is why many practitioners stick with defaults that work well across diverse workloads.

What performance bottlenecks are you facing in your LLM deployments? Understanding the prefill/decode dynamic might just hold the key to solving them.

Credits: Originally posted here: https://huggingface.co/blog/tngtech/llm-performance-prefill-decode-concurrent-requests
